analysis.one_liner: Bars bankruptcy courts from releasing government lawsuits against corporate executives and owners.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or vote on the bill, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company goes bankrupt, some bankruptcy courts have let courts' bankruptcy plans also wipe out lawsuits against people who never filed for bankruptcy themselves, like the company's owners or executives, even when states, cities, tribes, or the federal government are suing them. The bill would ban that: bankruptcy courts could not erase government claims against these non-debtors, and could pause those lawsuits for at most 90 days. The bill is named for the Sackler family, whose Purdue Pharma bankruptcy settlement sought to shield them from opioid lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments, federally recognized tribes, and the federal government would keep their ability to sue corporate owners and executives for wrongdoing even if the company files for bankruptcy. Opioid victims and their communities, whose representatives in government could then pursue the wealthy individuals behind the company, would benefit from that leverage. Everyday taxpayers would keep a path to recover from individuals who caused harm rather than being limited to a bankrupt company's empty coffers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Governments suing corporate executives and owners

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit bankruptcy courts from enjoining or releasing claims brought by states, municipalities, federally recognized tribes, or the United States against non-debtors, except for the special asbestos case provision at 11 U.S.C. 524(g).
Bankruptcy courts could still stay such lawsuits, but only for up to 90 days, so a bankrupt company cannot buy years of protection for its executives through the bankruptcy process.

The bill targets a practice with no clear legal footing: courts are split on whether they may release non-debtors' liability as part of a bankruptcy plan, and the bill would settle the question for government claimants by forbidding it.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy owners, executives, officers, and directors of companies facing government lawsuits would lose the ability to be released from liability through a bankruptcy settlement they did not personally consent to. Companies in complex bankruptcies might find settlements with governments harder to reach, since the individuals behind the company could no longer be fully protected in the deal.

drawbacks.text: Bankruptcy judges use non-debtor releases to get virtually every party to a dispute to agree to a global settlement; without the ability to release claims against owners and executives, some distressed companies might be unable to reach settlements at all, leaving victims with years of litigation instead of compensation.
The bill applies only to lawsuits by governments, so private victims' claims against non-debtors would still be releasable, which limits how much the bill actually protects individual plaintiffs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real imbalance: bankruptcy has become a route for wealthy owners to shed personal liability for corporate misconduct, and courts disagree on whether that is even allowed. The main cost is that some mass-tort settlements, including the Purdue Pharma settlement that paid billions to victims and governments, relied on non-debtor releases to close; blocking them for government claims could make such settlements harder to finalize and push money into prolonged litigation. On balance, the bill preserves governments' leverage against the individuals most responsible, which supporters judged worth that settlement friction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill on September 18, 2023, joined by Senators Warren and Welch.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was taken: the committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill received no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy company owners and executives facing government lawsuits, including the Sackler family's kind of arrangement, remain able to seek releases from liability through bankruptcy settlements, because the statute was never changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives shielded by bankruptcy settlement releases

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit bankruptcy courts from releasing government claims against non-debtors.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes, so the partisan split was never tested; all three sponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Corporate executives, owners, and directors facing government lawsuits
industries.note: The bill would strip away their ability to be released from government claims through a company's bankruptcy, keeping them personally exposed for corporate wrongdoing. Ordinary people gain when the wealthy individuals behind a bankrupt company cannot wipe out the government's case against them.

Global settlements that relied on releasing non-debtors to close would be harder to reach for government claimants, which could lengthen bankruptcy cases and litigation. That same difficulty is what preserves government leverage over the individuals involved.

A core tool of large corporate bankruptcy settlements, the non-debtor release, would be unavailable against government claimants, changing the economics of restructuring for troubled companies with litigation exposure.
